rules.title: High Buffer I/O Wait (PAGEIOLATCH)
rules.root_cause: PAGEIOLATCH waits mean SQL Server is waiting on physical disk I/O to bring data pages into the buffer pool. Common causes: buffer pool undersized for the working set (check Page Life Expectancy and Max Server Memory), missing or stale statistics causing more pages to be scanned than necessary, or genuine storage-layer I/O bottleneck.
resolution_steps: 1. Check Page Life Expectancy (mssql_perf_counters, counter_name='Page life expectancy') -- consistently low (under a few hundred seconds) points at buffer pool pressure
2. Check Max Server Memory (mssql_config_snapshot.max_server_memory_mb) against actual physical memory -- an undersized cap forces more physical reads
3. Check mssql_index_usage_delta for the affected database for missing/stale statistics or high leaf-level page churn
4. If storage-layer latency is suspected, check mssql_file_io_delta's io_stall_read_ms for the specific file

rules.title: High Lock Wait (Blocking Contention)
rules.root_cause: LCK_M_* waits mean sessions are waiting on locks held by other sessions -- genuine blocking, not I/O or CPU pressure. Common causes: long-running transactions holding locks longer than necessary, missing indexes forcing broader lock scope (table/page locks instead of row locks), or a genuinely high-concurrency hot row/page being contended.
resolution_steps: 1. Check mssql_blocking_snapshot for the same time period -- it captures the actual blocking_session_id/wait_resource/request_mode detail this wait-type-level rule can't see on its own
2. Look for long-running transactions (mssql_session_stats' cpu_time_ms/reads high relative to a short session count) that may be holding locks too long
3. Check for missing indexes on the contended table -- a missing index often forces a full scan under a lock that a seek would have avoided
4. Consider READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT isolation if blocking is between readers and writers specifically

rules.title: High Parallelism Wait (CXPACKET)
rules.root_cause: CXPACKET waits mean parallel query threads are waiting on each other to synchronize -- not necessarily a problem on its own (some CXPACKET is normal for genuinely parallel work), but high volume often means Cost Threshold for Parallelism is set too low (parallelizing cheap queries that shouldn't be) or Max Degree of Parallelism is mismatched to the workload.
resolution_steps: 1. Check mssql_config_snapshot.cost_threshold_for_parallelism -- the SQL Server default (5) is very low for most modern workloads; consider raising it (commonly 25-50) if this is genuinely default-configured
2. Check mssql_config_snapshot.max_dop against cpu_count -- an uncapped MAXDOP on a high-core-count server can cause excessive parallelism for small queries
3. Cross-reference with mssql_scheduler_stats' runnable_tasks_count -- if schedulers are already queued, added parallelism is making contention worse, not better

rules.title: High CPU Pressure (SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD)
rules.root_cause: SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD waits mean a task voluntarily yielded the CPU to let other tasks run and had to wait for its turn again -- this is a genuine CPU-pressure signal, distinct from I/O or lock waits. High volume means the instance's CPU is a bottleneck for the current workload, not any single query necessarily.
resolution_steps: 1. Check mssql_scheduler_stats' runnable_tasks_count across all schedulers -- consistently high values confirm genuine CPU saturation, not just one busy scheduler
2. Check mssql_plan_cache_stats for high-usecount plans with high total_worker_time_us -- these are the CPU-heaviest recurring queries worth tuning first

3. Check for excessive compilation (mssql_perf_counters, 'SQL Compilations/sec' and 'SQL Re-Compilations/sec') -- parameter sniffing or ad-hoc query volume can itself be a CPU drain independent of the queries' own logic

rules.title: High Buffer I/O Wait — Query Store
rules.root_cause: This specific query is spending a disproportionate share of its wait time on Buffer IO -- the per-query counterpart to MSSQL_WAIT_001's instance-wide signal, naming the actual query responsible rather than just the aggregate wait type. Same root causes apply (buffer pool pressure, missing/stale statistics, storage latency), but now attributable to one statement worth tuning directly.
resolution_steps: 1. Review this query's plan (mssql_qs_plan) for full/index scans that a covering index could avoid
2. Check whether the tables this query touches have current statistics
3. If the query is fundamentally I/O-bound by its nature (e.g. a genuine full-table reporting scan), confirm that's expected rather than accidental (a missing WHERE clause, for instance)

rules.title: High Lock Wait — Query Store
rules.root_cause: This specific query is spending a disproportionate share of its wait time waiting on locks -- the per-query counterpart to MSSQL_WAIT_002. Query Store's wait_category granularity can't say which other session or resource is the actual blocker (that detail only exists in mssql_blocking_snapshot, point-in-time, not per-query historically) -- this rule tells you WHICH query is most often the one waiting, not WHY.
resolution_steps: 1. Cross-reference mssql_blocking_snapshot around the times this query ran for the actual blocking_session_id/resource_type/request_mode detail
2. Check the query's own transaction scope -- is it doing more work inside the transaction than strictly necessary, holding locks longer than needed?
3. Check for a missing index that would let this query use a narrower row/page lock instead of a broader table lock

rules.title: High Parallel Exchange Port Synchronization Wait (CXSYNC_PORT)
rules.root_cause: CXSYNC_PORT (SQL Server 2022+) tracks time spent opening/closing/synchronizing the exchange ports parallel producer and consumer threads use to hand off rows -- introduced specifically to give this signal its own identity separate from CXPACKET. Unlike CXCONSUMER (the benign, expected side of parallelism, deliberately excluded from this rule engine's findings), high CXSYNC_PORT genuinely indicates workload imbalance: sustained port waits most often accompany a blocking operator -- a sort, hash build, or spool -- sitting between producer and consumer threads, so one stage of the plan gates the rest.
resolution_steps: 1. Identify the specific query/plan behind this wait (cross-reference mssql_qs_wait_stats/mssql_qs_plan for the same time window) and look for a blocking operator (Sort, Hash Match, Spool) feeding an exchange -- that operator's input is the real tuning target, not the wait itself
2. Check for skewed or misestimated row counts feeding the blocking operator -- fresh statistics often resolve this
3. Consider whether an index that provides the needed order could avoid the sort entirely
4. Review mssql_config_snapshot.cost_threshold_for_parallelism -- as with CXPACKET (MSSQL_WAIT_003), trivial queries going parallel unnecessarily can contribute

rules.title: High Transaction Log Write Wait (WRITELOG)
rules.root_cause: WRITELOG waits mean SQL Server is waiting for the transaction log buffer to be flushed to disk -- charged on every COMMIT, on CHECKPOINT, and whenever a log block fills. Two genuinely different root causes produce this signal, distinguishable by which metric is driving the finding: a LOW avg_wait_ms alongside a high wait_pct_of_total points at commit FREQUENCY -- many small, individually-committed transactions each waiting only briefly, but accumulating into a large total simply from volume (batching/commit-frequency issue, not a storage problem). A HIGH avg_wait_ms specifically points at genuine transaction log I/O latency -- the storage subsystem itself is slow to harden each write, regardless of how many there are.
resolution_steps: 1. Check avg_wait_ms specifically: low (a few ms or less) with high volume suggests batching many small transactions into fewer, larger commits, or considering delayed durability (SQL Server 2014+) if the application can tolerate the small window of potential data loss on crash

2. High avg_wait_ms (double digits or more) suggests genuine storage-layer latency -- check mssql_file_io_delta's io_stall_write_ms for the transaction log file specifically, and confirm the log file is on fast, dedicated storage, not shared with data files or other I/O-heavy workloads
3. If using Availability Groups in synchronous commit mode, also check for HADR_SYNC_COMMIT -- the remote log copy can itself introduce this same class of delay, separate from local disk latency
4. Confirm CHECKPOINT frequency isn't excessive (mssql_perf_counters, 'Log Flushes/sec' and related counters) if commits alone don't explain the volume

rules.title: High Transaction Log Write Wait — Query Store
rules.root_cause: This specific query is spending a disproportionate share of its wait time on transaction log writes -- the per-query counterpart to MSSQL_WAIT_008's instance-wide signal. Query Store attributes this to whichever query's commit (or the transaction it participates in) triggered the log flush, naming the actual statement responsible rather than just the aggregate wait type.
resolution_steps: 1. Check whether this query commits frequently within a loop or batch (e.g. row-by-row processing with a commit per row) -- consolidating into fewer, larger transactions is often the most direct fix

2. Cross-reference mssql_wait_type's WRITELOG avg_wait_ms (MSSQL_WAIT_008) to determine whether this is a frequency issue (many small commits) or a genuine storage-latency issue affecting this query's commits specifically
3. If this query's transaction includes other write-heavy statements, confirm none of them are generating unexpectedly large log volume (e.g. an unintended full-table UPDATE)

rules.title: High Memory Grant Wait — Query Store
rules.root_cause: Query Store's Memory wait category is the query-level view of RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE waits -- a query's memory grant request (needed for sorts, hash joins, and similar memory-intensive operators) couldn't be satisfied immediately because other concurrent queries were holding the memory instead. This is a genuinely serious signal, not routine contention: Microsoft's own documentation for RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE explicitly calls out 'excessive number of concurrent queries, or excessive memory request amounts' as the cause, and it can escalate to query timeout error 8645 if the wait is long enough.
resolution_steps: 1. Check whether this query's plan (mssql_qs_plan) involves a large Sort or Hash Match -- these are what actually request the memory grant; a missing index that would avoid the sort/hash is often the most direct fix
2. Check whether stale statistics are causing an inflated cardinality estimate and therefore an oversized memory grant request -- update statistics on the tables involved
3. Check mssql_perf_counters for 'Memory Grants Pending' (high) and 'Memory Grants Outstanding' (low) -- confirms genuine memory-grant contention rather than a one-off

4. If many concurrent queries are competing for memory rather than one query being the culprit, consider Resource Governor memory limits, or MIN_GRANT_PERCENT/MAX_GRANT_PERCENT query hints (SQL Server 2012 SP3+) to cap how much any single query can request
5. Confirm mssql_config_snapshot.max_server_memory_mb isn't set low enough to be the real constraint before assuming this is purely a query-tuning problem

rules.title: High Network I/O Wait (ASYNC_NETWORK_IO)
rules.root_cause: ASYNC_NETWORK_IO means SQL Server has results ready to send but is waiting for the CLIENT to consume them over the network -- despite the name, this is very often not a network problem at all. The most common cause by far is the application/client fetching rows too slowly (row-by-row processing in a loop instead of bulk fetch, a chatty ORM, or a client-side cursor pulling one row at a time), not genuine network latency or bandwidth.
resolution_steps: 1. Check whether the client application is processing result sets row-by-row rather than in bulk -- this is the most common root cause, not the network itself
2. Confirm the query isn't returning far more rows/columns than the application actually uses -- trimming an unnecessarily wide or long result set reduces the transfer burden
3. If genuine network latency is suspected (e.g. cross-region client), check mssql_session_stats' client_net_address to confirm whether affected sessions are consistently remote
4. Rule out the client application pausing mid-fetch to do per-row work (logging, UI updates) before requesting the next row

rules.title: High In-Memory Page Latch Wait (PAGELATCH)
rules.root_cause: PAGELATCH waits (not to be confused with PAGEIOLATCH) are for a page already IN MEMORY -- no disk I/O involved. The classic cause is 'last page insert contention': many concurrent sessions inserting into the same table's last page (an ever-increasing identity/sequential key with no natural spread), all fighting over the same in-memory page structure. Heavy TempDB object creation/allocation churn is the other common cause.
resolution_steps: 1. For insert-heavy tables with a sequential/identity key: consider a different distribution (a hash/GUID-leading key, or multiple last-page 'hot spots' via partitioning) to spread inserts across more pages

2. Check mssql_tempdb_session_usage/mssql_tempdb_task_usage for the same time window -- heavy temp table creation/dropping is a common concurrent cause of this same wait, distinct from the insert-contention scenario

3. Confirm TempDB has multiple data files configured (one per CPU core, up to ~8, is the standard guidance) -- a single TempDB data file is a well-known amplifier of PAGELATCH contention specifically in TempDB

rules.title: High Memory Grant Wait — Instance-Wide (RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE)
rules.root_cause: The instance-wide counterpart to MSSQL_WAIT_010's Query Store Memory-category signal. A query's memory grant request (for sorts, hash joins, and similar memory-intensive operators) couldn't be satisfied immediately because other concurrent queries were holding the memory instead. Genuinely serious per Microsoft's own documentation -- can escalate to query timeout error 8645 if sustained.
resolution_steps: 1. Cross-reference MSSQL_WAIT_010's Query Store Memory-category findings if any exist for the same period -- that identifies WHICH query is driving this, this instance-wide signal only confirms THAT it's happening
2. Check mssql_perf_counters for 'Memory Grants Pending' (high) and 'Memory Grants Outstanding' (low) to confirm sustained contention rather than a brief spike
3. Look for missing indexes or stale statistics driving oversized sort/hash memory requests across multiple queries, not just one
4. Confirm mssql_config_snapshot.max_server_memory_mb isn't constraining the instance below what the workload genuinely needs

rules.title: High Non-Buffer I/O Completion Wait (IO_COMPLETION)
rules.root_cause: IO_COMPLETION covers I/O outside the normal buffer-pool page-read path that PAGEIOLATCH tracks -- most commonly backup/restore I/O, or reads during operations like DBCC CHECKDB. High values during a backup window are expected and not a concern; high values OUTSIDE any known backup/maintenance window point at genuine storage-layer latency for whatever operation is running.
resolution_steps: 1. First confirm whether this coincides with a scheduled backup, restore, or consistency-check (DBCC CHECKDB) window -- if so, this is expected, not a finding requiring action
2. If it does NOT coincide with known maintenance activity, check mssql_file_io_delta's io_stall_read_ms/io_stall_write_ms for the affected database's files to confirm genuine storage latency
3. Check whether multiple large operations (backups, bulk loads, index rebuilds) are running concurrently and competing for the same storage I/O capacity

rules.title: High Availability Group Synchronous Commit Wait (HADR_SYNC_COMMIT)
rules.root_cause: HADR_SYNC_COMMIT is specific to Always On Availability Groups running in synchronous-commit mode -- the primary replica waits for confirmation that the transaction log record has been hardened to disk on ALL synchronous secondary replicas before the commit can return to the caller. High waits here mean a secondary replica (or the network path to it) is the bottleneck, not the primary's own local storage.
resolution_steps: 1. Check network latency and throughput between the primary and each synchronous secondary replica -- this is the most common root cause
2. Check the secondary replica(s)' own local storage/log-write performance -- a slow secondary's local WRITELOG-equivalent delay propagates directly into this wait on the primary
3. Confirm whether a specific secondary is consistently the slow one (worth investigating in isolation) versus all secondaries contributing roughly equally
4. Consider whether this replica genuinely needs synchronous commit, or whether asynchronous commit is acceptable for its role, if the durability guarantee isn't strictly required

rules.title: High Exclusive Latch Wait on Non-Page Structures (LATCH_EX)
rules.root_cause: LATCH_EX is for an exclusive latch on a non-page internal structure -- distinct from PAGELATCH (in-memory data pages) and PAGEIOLATCH (disk page reads). Common causes include a data or log file needing to autogrow (the growth operation itself briefly serializes access), or internal metadata structure contention unrelated to any specific table's data.
resolution_steps: 1. Check whether database/log file autogrow events are occurring frequently during the affected window -- pre-sizing files appropriately and avoiding small autogrow increments reduces this

2. If autogrow isn't the cause, this often requires deeper investigation via sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks captured live during the issue, since LATCH_EX covers a broad range of internal structures not identifiable from aggregate wait stats alone
3. Confirm Instant File Initialization is enabled (reduces the time a data file growth operation takes, though it does not help log file growth)

rules.title: High Windows Authentication Call Wait (PREEMPTIVE_OS_AUTHENTICATIONOPS)
rules.root_cause: SQL Server hands control out to an external Windows authentication API call for this wait -- small values are routine and expected (confirmed against multiple DBA sources), but genuinely high or sustained values can indicate a real Active Directory/Domain Controller performance or connectivity problem, since every authentication check has to round-trip to AD. This is deliberately NOT in this rule engine's benign-wait exclusion list, unlike most other PREEMPTIVE_OS_* waits, specifically because it can be a real signal at scale where those are not.
resolution_steps: 1. Check whether Domain Controller response times or connectivity have degraded around the same period -- this is the most likely root cause if the value is genuinely high, not sporadic

2. Check whether authentication volume itself has increased (e.g. connection pooling misconfigured, causing far more login/authentication events than expected) rather than DC performance itself degrading

3. If this is intermittent and low-magnitude, it's very likely not a real problem -- this rule's threshold is intentionally set to only fire on a sustained, meaningful share of total wait time, not routine background authentication activity
